newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - January 29.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - January 29.

text.p: - Prepared by The Broadcast Monitoring Company for Reuters
-- CLARKE REAFFIRMS EMU STANCE

Chancellor Kenneth Clarke has challenged Eurosceptics in the Tory party by reaffirming his contention that Britain could still be among the first wave of countries to join a single European currency in 1999. Interviewed by the Financial Times, Clarke suggested that were the launch of Emu to be delayed by just six months from its present date of January 1 1999, Britain might well join. His comments are still in line with the current Cabinet position that monetary union is "very unlikely" to take place on the January 1 1999 deadline.
-- LABOUR UNLIKELY TO OPT FOR EMU ENTRY AT LAUNCH

Robin Cook, the shadow foreign secretary, has said that the Labour party is already preparing European Union member states for a British decision not to join the first wave of European monetary union in 1999. Interviewed in the Financial Times, Cook said he had already discussed the issue with leading figures in European centre-left parties. Cook also said that a Labour government would use Britain's EU presidency in the first half of 1998 to push forward the twin objectives of EU enlargement and the completion of the single market.
-- GRADE SET TO TAKE TOP JOB AT FIRST LEISURE

Michael Grade, whose surprise resignation as chief executive of Channel 4 earlier this week shocked the television industry, is planning to join First Leisure Corp Plc as full-time executive chairman. Grade is expected to make a formal announcement soon.
-- BEIJING BUYS STAKE IN TOP HONG KONG POWER SUPPLIER

The Chinese government is set to pay HK$16.25 billion (1.3 billion stg) to take a 20 per cent stake in China Light & Power, one of the biggest utilities in Hong Kong. The purchase by Citic Pacific, the Hong Kong arm of the Chinese government, is part of Beijing's strategy of expanding its infrastructure activities in Hong Kong ahead of the territory's return to China on June 30 at midnight.
-- UK EXPORTS TO NON-EU COUNTRIES SHOW STEEP FALL

Figures from the Office of National Statistics show that British exports to countries outside the European Union recorded the biggest fall in nine years last month. The figures show that Britain's trade gap widened to a seasonally-adjusted 959 million stg in November, compared to 680 million stg in October. The fall was worse than City expectations, and underscores the difficulties faced by companies coping with a strong pound.
-- BOOKER WINS 400 MLN STG ARMY FOOD CONTRACT FROM NAAFI

The Naafi, the traditional supplier to the British military, has lost a 400 million stg contract to supply food to the armed forces. British food distribution company Booker beat Naafi to the five-year contract following a 12-month tendering process. -- EXPORTS HELP LIFT ROVER SALES OVER 500,000 UNITS

British car maker Rover sold 507,254 units last year, of which 54 percent were exports. The figures compare with 49 percent exported in 1995, with new models largely accounting for the rise in foreign registrations. The 1996 figures are the first time since 1988 that Rover has sold over 500,000 units in a year, with the total number of new registrations rising by five percent compared to 1995.
-- SWITCH TO LAUNCH COMPUTER-BACKED DEBIT CARD

Switch, the British debit card consortium founded by National Westminster Bank, Midland Bank and Royal Bank of Scotland, is set to launch a new computer-backed payment card called Solo. The card, which requires every payment to be authorised by computer, is similar to the Electron card offered by the rival Visa consortium, which also requires each transaction to be authorised online. Switch estimates that Solo could reach 3.3 million people in the next 12 months, and 8.0 million over three years.
-- LUCASVARITY EYES DIVIDEND REFORM

LucasVarity, the Anglo-US engineering group created by the 3.2 billion stg merger last year of Varity Corporation of the United States and Britain's Lucas Industries, has suggested that it might reduce dividend payments and reward investors with share buy-backs instead. Such a move would place LucasVarity among the first British quoted companies to move away from using dividend payments to return value to investors. The group says it will first discuss the proposals with leading institutional shareholders.
-- NOVARTIS PLANS BIG INCREASE IN PAYOUTS

Novartis, the pharmaceutical giant created by the merger of Swiss drugs groups Ciba Geigy and Sandoz, has said it plans to increase its dividends to more than 30 percent of retained earnings. The proposals, announced by Novartis chief executive Daniel Vasalla in an interview with the Financial Times, come in response to the group's strong balance sheet and the tax implications for shareholders of buying back its own shares.
